meaning: two days before yesterday, three days ago
headline: Sakiototoi is 先 (saki, “previous”) plus 一昨日 (ototoi, “day before yesterday”); the kanji spelling is jukujikun.

sources.quote: Compound of 先(さき) (saki, “previous”) + 一昨日(おととい) (ototoi, “day before yesterday”).
The kanji spelling is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

headline: Koshi first appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *kəsi.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE. In turn from Proto-Japonic *kəsi.

headline: Mata is from Proto-Japonic *mata, cognate with Miyako and Okinawan mata.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mata. Cognate with Miyako 股 (また, mata), Okinawan 股 (また, mata).

headline: Tsutome is the continuative stem of 勤める (tsutomeru).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 勤(つと)める (tsutomeru).

headline: Maru shifted from Old Japanese 丸 (maro), and is related to 麻呂 (maro).

sources.quote: ⟨maro₂⟩ → */marə/ → /maru/
Shift from Old Japanese 丸 (maro, see below).
Related to 麻(ま)呂(ろ) (maro).

headline: Higeki is a calque of English tragedy, built from 悲 (hi, “sad, sorrowful”) plus 劇 (geki, “drama; play”).

sources.quote: Calque of English tragedy, from Middle Chinese-derived elements 悲(ひ) (hi, “sad, sorrowful”) + 劇(げき) (geki, “drama; play”).

headline: Sumai is the continuative stem of 住まう (sumau, “to live at; to dwell; to reside”), first attested in the 970s.

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 住(す)まう (sumau, “to live at; to dwell; to reside”).
First attested in the 970s.

meaning: to store to pay, to supply
headline: Osameru is cognate with 治める (osameru) and 修める (osameru).

sources.quote: Cognate with Japanese 治(おさ)める (osameru) and 修(おさ)める (osameru).

meaning: to exchange, to interchange, to substitute
headline: This kaeru, written 換, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the lower bigrade pattern.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 変(か)える (kaeru), 替(か)える (kaeru) and 代(か)える (kaeru).

headline: Zōsen is Middle Chinese 造船.

sources.quote: Middle Chinese 造船

headline: Marugoto is 丸 (maru, “round; (by extension) entirety”) plus ごと (-goto).

sources.quote: Compound of 丸 (maru, “round; (by extension) entirety”) + ごと (-goto).

meaning: to jump in, to leap in, to plunge into
headline: Tobikomu is tobi, the stem of 飛ぶ (tobu, “to jump; to fly”), plus 込む (komu, “to go into”).

sources.quote: Compound of 飛(と)び (tobi, “jumping”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 飛(と)ぶ (tobu, “to jump; to fly”)) + 込(こ)む (komu, “to go into”).

headline: Chōjo is 長 (“long; elder”) plus 女 (“woman; female”).

sources.quote: Compound of 長 (“long; elder”) + 女 (“woman; female”).

headline: Shū, “week”, is from Middle Chinese 周 (MC tsyuw).

sources.quote: /t͡ɕɨu/ → /ɕjɨu/ → /ɕuː/
From Middle Chinese 周 (MC tsyuw).

headline: Shizen kagaku is 自然 (shizen, “nature”) plus 科学 (kagaku, “science”).

sources.quote: 自然 (shizen, “nature”) + 科学 (kagaku, “science”)

headline: Shōgi is first attested in the Shinsarugakuki (11th century) as 將基, and is probably cognate with Chinese 象棋 (xiàngqí).

sources.quote: First attested in Shinsarugakuki (11th century) as 將基, but also later as 象戯 or 象棋 in other literatures. Probably cognate with Chinese 象棋 (xiàngqí).

headline: Shi, “poem”, is from Middle Chinese 詩 (MC syi).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 詩 (MC syi).

headline: Sukī is borrowed from English ski, from Norwegian ski.

sources.quote: Borrowed from English ski, from Norwegian ski.

meaning: Thank you; somehow; no matter how hard one may try
headline: Dōmo is どう (dō, “how”) plus も (mo, “ever, even, also”): close in meaning to “no matter how”.

sources.quote: Derived as compound of どう (dō, “how”, question word) + も (mo, “ever, even, also”, particle). Literal meaning is close to “no matter how, howsoever, in all cases”. Idiomatically and semantically used as an intensifier in specific contexts. Compare とても (totemo, “very”).

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Iroiro is a reduplication of 色 (iro, “colour; type; kind”).

sources.quote: Reduplication of 色(いろ) (iro, “colour; type; kind”).

headline: Shimekiri is the stem of 締め切る (shimekiru): 締め (shime, “fastening, locking, shutting”) plus 切り (kiri).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 締(し)め切(き)る (shimekiru). By surface analysis, 締(し)め (shime, “fastening, locking, shutting”) + 切(き)り (kiri).

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 意識 (ʔiH syik).

headline: Hikidasu is hiki, the stem of 引く (hiku, “to pull”), plus 出す (dasu, “to take out”).

sources.quote: Compound of 引き (hiki, the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 引く (hiku), “to pull”) + 出す (dasu, “to take out”).

headline: Sukima is 隙 (suki, “gap”) plus 間 (ma, “space”).

sources.quote: 隙(すき) (suki, “gap”) + 間(ま) (ma, “space”)

headline: Tatoe is perhaps from たとい (tatoi).

sources.quote: Perhaps from たとい (tatoi).

headline: Take, “bamboo”, has several derivation theories, one linking it to words for height: 高 (taka), 長 (take), 丈 (take).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *takai.
Theories on derivation include:
* From 長(たけ)生(おう) (takeou) or 高(たか)生(はえ) (takahae), in reference to the speed at which bamboo grows.
* Cognate with 高(たか) (taka), 長(たけ) (take), 丈(たけ) (take), all “height”.
* From 高(たか)景(かけ) (takakake) or つらこえ (tsurakoe).
* From ta meaning “tall” (高(たか)い (takai)) + ke, ancient combining form of 木(き) (ki, “tree”).
* A contraction of 痛(いた)快(く)茎(き)延(は)へ (itakukihae), referring to the speed at which bamboo grows.
* From ta, from Korean 대 (dae, “bamboo”) (see also 대나무 (daenamu, “bamboo”, literally “bamboo tree”)), + ke, ancient combining form of 木(き) (ki).

meaning: Take care of yourself, Take care!, Get well soon
headline: Odaiji ni is お (o) plus 大事 (daiji, “important”) plus に (ni), shortened from お大事になさってください (o daiji ni nasatte kudasai).

sources.quote: From お (o, honorific marker) + 大(だい)事(じ) (daiji, “important”) + に (ni, particle for direction); shortened from expressions such as お大(だい)事(じ)になさってください (o daiji ni nasatte kudasai, “Please take care of yourself”).

headline: Ageru is from Old Japanese 上ぐ (agu), from Proto-Japonic *ank-a-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 上ぐ (agu), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”), from Proto-Japonic *ank-a-.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Ueru is from the classical verb 植う (uu).

sources.quote: */uwu/ → /uweru/ → /ueru/
From classical verb 植う (uu).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Fukuro is very likely related to 含む (fukumu, “to include”) and 膨れる (fukureru, “to swell”), from a root *puk-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *pukoro.
Very likely related to 含む (fukumu, “to include”), also among others deriving from a root *puk- (e.g. 膨れる (fukureru, “to swell”)).
